title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Symposium Summary on Issues Concerning the Application of Legal Norms in the Adjudication of Administrative Cases
keywords_en: Administrative litigation; Adjudication of administrative cases
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the "Summary of the Symposium on Issues Concerning the Application of Legal Norms in the Trial of Administrative Cases"

Fa [2004] No. 96

To the High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government, and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

The "Summary of the Symposium on Issues Concerning the Application of Legal Norms in the Trial of Administrative Cases" is hereby issued for your reference and implementation. Please promptly report any issues encountered during implementation to this Court.

May 18, 2004

Summary of the Symposium on Issues Concerning the Application of Legal Norms in the Trial of Administrative Cases

Administrative adjudication involves a relatively large number of levels and categories of legal norms. Since the implementation of the Legislation Law, the rules on the application of law have also undergone significant changes. In the application of law, various difficult issues are often encountered, such as how to identify the legal basis and resolve conflicts between legal norms. Whether these issues can be properly resolved directly affects the fairness and efficiency of administrative adjudication. Moreover, with the improvement of China's rule of law level and the need to adapt to WTO accession, the role of administrative adjudication in resolving conflicts of legal norms and maintaining the unity of the legal system has become increasingly prominent. In order to accurately apply legal norms, ensure the fair trial of administrative cases, safeguard the unity and dignity of the national legal system, and promote law-based administration, the Administrative Adjudication Tribunal of the Supreme People's Court previously conducted a special investigation and research on prominent issues concerning the application of legal norms in the trial of administrative cases and sought opinions from relevant departments. In October 2003, during the National Conference on Administrative Adjudication Work of Courts held in Shanghai by the Supreme People's Court, a special symposium was held on issues concerning the application of legal norms in the trial of administrative cases. On the basis of summarizing trial experience, and in accordance with the Legislation Law, the Administrative Procedure Law, and other relevant legal provisions, the participants reached a consensus on some common issues. The relevant contents are hereby summarized as follows:

I. The Basis for Adjudication of Administrative Cases

In accordance with the relevant provisions of the Administrative Procedure Law and the Legislation Law, when trying administrative cases, the people's courts shall base their decisions on laws, administrative regulations, local regulations, autonomous regulations, and separate regulations, and shall refer to rules. When referring to rules, the court shall determine whether the provisions of the rules are lawful and effective, and shall apply lawful and effective rules. In accordance with the provisions of the Legislation Law, the Regulations on Procedures for the Formulation of Administrative Regulations, and the Regulations on Procedures for the Formulation of Rules concerning the interpretation of laws, administrative regulations, and rules, the legal interpretations of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, and the interpretations of administrative regulations published by the State Council or departments authorized by the State Council, shall be used as the legal basis for the people's courts in trying administrative cases; interpretations of rules made by the rule-making authority that have the same effect as the rules shall be applied by reference when the people's courts try administrative cases.

Considering the evolution of China's legislative procedures since the founding of the People's Republic, currently effective administrative regulations fall into the following three categories: First, administrative regulations formulated and published by the State Council; Second, administrative regulations published by departments of the State Council with the approval of the State Council in accordance with the procedures for formulating administrative regulations that were effective before the implementation of the Legislation Law. However, after the implementation of the Legislation Law, normative documents published by departments of the State Council with the approval of the State Council are no longer considered administrative regulations; Third, other administrative regulations confirmed by the State Council during the cleanup of administrative regulations.

In the practice of administrative adjudication, specific application interpretations and other normative documents issued by relevant departments to guide the implementation of laws or administrative measures are often involved. These mainly include: interpretations made by departments of the State Council, as well as the people's governments of provinces, autonomous regions, municipalities directly under the Central Government, and larger cities, or their competent departments, on the specific application of laws, regulations, or rules; decisions, orders, or other normative documents of general binding force formulated and issued by people's governments at or above the county level or their competent departments. Administrative organs often use these specific application interpretations and other normative documents as the direct basis for specific administrative acts. These specific application interpretations and normative documents are not formal sources of law and have no binding force on the people's courts in the sense of legal norms. However, if, upon examination, the people's court finds that the specific application interpretations and other normative documents on which the specific administrative act under suit is based are lawful, effective, reasonable, and appropriate, the court shall recognize their validity when determining the legality of the specific administrative act under suit; the people's court may comment in the reasoning of the judgment on whether the specific application interpretations and other normative documents are lawful, effective, reasonable, or appropriate.

II. Rules for the Application of Conflicting Legal Norms

When two or more legal norms regulating the same subject matter conflict because they prescribe different legal consequences, generally, the applicable legal norms shall be determined and selected in accordance with the rules of legal application stipulated in the Legislation Law, such as the supremacy of higher-level law over lower-level law, the later law prevailing over the earlier law, and the special law prevailing over the general law. If the matter involved in the conflicting norms is relatively significant, the relevant authorities have different opinions on whether a conflict exists, the lawfulness and validity of the legal norm that should be given priority are questionable, or it cannot be determined which norm to apply according to the rules of legal application, the matter shall be submitted level by level to the competent authority for a ruling in accordance with the procedures stipulated in the Legislation Law.

(A) Determination and Application of Lower-Level Law Not in Conformity with Higher-Level Law

If the provisions of a lower-level law do not conform to a higher-level law, the people's court shall, in principle, apply the higher-level law. Currently, many specific administrative acts are made based on lower-level laws without citing or applying the higher-level law. Under such circumstances, in order to maintain the unity of the legal system, when reviewing the legality of a specific administrative act, the people's court shall also determine whether the lower-level law conforms to the higher-level law. If it is determined that the lower-level law conflicts with the higher-level law, the legality of the specific administrative act under suit shall be determined based on the higher-level law. From trial practice, common situations where lower-level law does not conform to higher-level law include: the lower-level law narrows the scope of rights subjects stipulated in the higher-level law, or expands the scope of rights subjects stipulated in the higher-level law in violation of the legislative purpose of the higher-level law; the lower-level law restricts or deprives of the rights stipulated in the higher-level law, or expands the scope of rights stipulated in the higher-level law in violation of the legislative purpose of the higher-level law; the lower-level law expands the scope of administrative subjects or their functions and powers; the lower-level law extends the time limit for performing statutory duties stipulated in the higher-level law; the lower-level law expands or narrows the scope, nature, or conditions of obligations or obligation subjects stipulated in the higher-level law by means of reference, analogous application, etc.; the lower-level law adds or narrows the conditions for application that violate the higher-level law; the lower-level law expands or narrows the scope, types, and ranges of administrative penalties for conduct stipulated in the higher-level law; the lower-level law changes the nature of illegal acts already stipulated in the higher-level law; the lower-level law exceeds the scope, types, and methods of compulsory measures stipulated in the higher-level law, and adds or narrows the conditions for their application; laws, regulations, rules, or other normative documents establish administrative permits that do not comply with the Administrative Permit Law, or add conditions for administrative permits that violate the higher-level law; other conflicting situations.

After a law, administrative regulation, or local regulation is amended, if its implementing provisions have not been expressly abolished, the people's court shall, when applying them, distinguish the following situations: if the implementing provisions conflict with the amended law, administrative regulation, or local regulation, they shall not be applied; if, due to the amendment of the law, administrative regulation, or local regulation, the corresponding implementing provisions lose their basis and cannot be implemented independently, they shall not be applied; if the implementing provisions do not conflict with the amended law, administrative regulation, or local regulation, they may be applied.

(B) The Relationship Between Special Provisions and General Provisions

If different articles within the same law, administrative regulation, local regulation, autonomous regulation, separate regulation, or rule contain both general provisions and special provisions on the same matter, the special provisions shall prevail.

If new general provisions conflict with old special provisions on the same matter between laws, between administrative regulations, or between local regulations, the people's court shall, in principle, apply them according to the following situations: if the new general provisions allow the old special provisions to continue to apply, the old special provisions shall apply; if the new general provisions abolish the old special provisions, the new general provisions shall apply. If it cannot be determined whether the new general provisions allow the old provisions to continue to apply, the people's court shall suspend the trial of the administrative case; if it involves a law, the matter shall be reported level by level to the Supreme People's Court, which shall refer it to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for a ruling; if it involves an administrative regulation, the matter shall be reported level by level to the Supreme People's Court, which shall refer it to the State Council for a ruling; if it involves a local regulation, the matter shall be referred by the High People's Court to the enacting authority for a ruling.

(C) Selection and Application in Case of Conflict Between Local Regulations and Departmental Rules

If the provisions of a local regulation and a departmental rule on the same matter are inconsistent, the people's court may generally apply them according to the following situations: (1) If a law or administrative regulation authorizes a departmental rule to make implementing provisions, those provisions shall prevail; (2) If no law or administrative regulation has been formulated, the provisions of a departmental rule concerning matters authorized by the decisions or orders of the State Council, or concerning matters of central macro-control, market activity rules requiring national uniformity, and matters such as foreign trade and foreign investment that require uniform national provisions, shall prevail; (3) If a local regulation, based on the authorization of a law or administrative regulation, makes specific provisions according to the actual circumstances of its administrative region, those provisions shall prevail; (4) Provisions made by a local regulation on matters falling within local affairs shall prevail; (5) If no law or administrative regulation has been formulated, provisions made by a local regulation according to the specific circumstances of its administrative region on matters other than those requiring uniform national provisions shall prevail; (6) Other situations where direct application is possible. If it cannot be determined which to apply, the trial of the administrative case shall be suspended, and the matter shall be reported level by level to the Supreme People's Court, which shall refer it to the competent authority for handling in accordance with Article 86, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the Legislation Law.

(D) Selection and Application in Case of Conflict Between Rules

If the provisions of a departmental rule and a local government rule on the same matter are inconsistent, the people's court may generally apply them according to the following situations: (1) If a law or administrative regulation authorizes a departmental rule to make implementing provisions, those provisions shall prevail; (2) If no law or administrative regulation has been formulated, the provisions of a departmental rule concerning matters authorized by the decisions or orders of the State Council, or concerning matters of central macro-control, market activity rules requiring national uniformity, and matters such as foreign trade and foreign investment, shall prevail; (3) If a local government rule, based on the authorization of a law or administrative regulation, makes specific provisions according to the actual circumstances of its administrative region, those provisions shall prevail; (4) Provisions made by a local government rule on specific administrative management matters within its administrative region shall prevail; (5) Other situations where direct application is possible. If it cannot be determined which to apply, the trial of the administrative case shall be suspended, and the matter shall be reported level by level to the Supreme People's Court, which shall refer it to the State Council for a ruling.

If the provisions of rules formulated by different departments of the State Council on the same matter are inconsistent, the people's court may generally select and apply them according to the following situations: (1) Apply the provisions of the departmental rule that does not conflict with the higher-level law; (2) If neither conflicts with the higher-level law, the provisions of the rule formulated based on exclusive functions and powers shall prevail; (3) Provisions jointly formulated by two or more departments of the State Council on matters falling within their respective functional scopes shall prevail over provisions made individually by one of the departments; (4) Other situations where selection and application are possible. If it cannot be determined which to apply, the trial of the administrative case shall be suspended, and the matter shall be reported level by level to the Supreme People's Court, which shall refer it to the State Council for a ruling.

If the provisions of other normative documents formulated by departments of the State Council or the people's governments of provinces, autonomous regions, or municipalities directly under the Central Government on the same matter are inconsistent, the above principles shall be applied by reference.

III. Rules for the Application of New and Old Legal Norms

According to the common understanding and practice in administrative adjudication, when the conduct of an administrative counterpart occurred before the implementation of a new law, and the specific administrative act was made after the implementation of the new law, when the people's court reviews the legality of the specific administrative act, substantive issues shall be governed by the old law, and procedural issues shall be governed by the new law, except in the following circumstances: (1) otherwise provided by laws, regulations, or rules; (2) applying the new law is more favorable for protecting the lawful rights and interests of the administrative counterpart; (3) the nature of the specific administrative act requires the application of the substantive provisions of the new law.

IV. Issues Concerning the Interpretation of Specific Application of Legal Norms

Interpreting legal norms in adjudicating cases is an important part of the people's court's application of law. The people's court shall generally interpret the applicable legal norms according to their usual meaning; if there is a special professional meaning, that meaning shall prevail; if the meaning is unclear or ambiguous, it may be determined based on the context, legislative intent, purpose, and principles.

When a legal norm enumerates typical matters to which it applies and then uses expressions such as "etc." or "other" to describe them, it constitutes an incomplete enumeration of illustrative provisions. Matters expressed by general terms such as "etc." or "other" are matters other than those expressly enumerated, and the circumstances so summarized shall be similar to the enumerated matters.

When interpreting and applying the law, the people's court shall properly handle the relationship between legal effect and social effect. It shall strictly apply legal provisions and safeguard the seriousness of the law, ensuring the certainty, uniformity, and continuity of legal application, while also keeping pace with the times, paying attention to the social effect of handling cases, avoiding rigid and mechanical understanding and application of legal provisions, and safeguarding national interests and social public interests in the application of law.
